questions.question_text: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of $x^{2}-6x+4=0$, what is the value of $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$?

options.why: Evaluated $(\alpha+\beta)^2$ without subtracting $2\alpha\beta$.
Added $2\alpha\beta$ instead of subtracting it from $(\alpha+\beta)^2$.
Subtracted $4\alpha\beta$ instead of $2\alpha\beta$ from the squared sum.

questions.question_text:
The roots of $x^{3}-5x^{2}+3x-2=0$ are $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$.
What is $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\gamma^{2}$?

options.why: Evaluated $(\sum\alpha)^2$ only, omitting $-2\sum\alpha\beta$.
Added $2\sum\alpha\beta$ instead of subtracting it from the squared sum.
Subtracted $4\sum\alpha\beta$ instead of $2\sum\alpha\beta$ from the squared sum.

questions.question_text:

options.why: Multiplied the product of roots by $3$ instead of $3^2=9$.
Did not scale the sum of roots by the factor $3$.

The line $y=x+3$ meets the parabola $y=x^{2}-7x+10$ at $A$ and $B$.
What is the $x$-coordinate of the midpoint of $AB$?

options.why: Found the sum of the roots $\alpha+\beta$ without dividing by $2$.

questions.question_text: For the equation $x^{2}-4x+9=0$, what is the value of $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$, and what does this imply about the roots?

options.text: $34$; the roots are real and distinct.
options.why: Added $2\alpha\beta$ instead of subtracting it from $(\alpha+\beta)^2$.

options.text: $-2$; the roots are real and equal.
options.why: Misinterpreted a negative sum of squares as indicating equal roots.
Omitted the $2\alpha\beta$ term entirely when evaluating the sum of squares.

questions.solution_text:
$\alpha+\beta=4, \alpha\beta=9$
$\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=4^{2}-2(9)$
$=16-18$
$=-2$
Since the sum of squares is negative, the roots are not real.

questions.question_text:
